drills.q: What defect-density reduction range do cited industrial TDD case studies (IBM, Microsoft) report?
True or false: a CI gate that requires a new test for new logic guarantees the test is high quality.
drills.a: False -- it only enforces that a test exists (the mechanical form of the practice), not that its assertions actually verify behavior. A mutation-testing audit is needed to check quality.

drills.q: What's the one genuine PREREQUISITE (not refinement) chaos engineering needs before it's safe to run at all?
drills.a: Mature observability and a fast, tested rollback/abort mechanism.

drills.q: Explain the 2026-specific argument for writing a test before delegating implementation to an AI coding agent.
drills.a: A failing test is a falsifiable oracle the agent can build against; a vague natural-language prompt gives the agent no such oracle, and its documented failure mode is confidently building on a wrong assumption rather than asking for clarification.

drills.q: A team announces 'we do TDD now' but a code-shape audit shows tests written after implementation, matching it line for line. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: No enforcement mechanism -- the practice depended on individual discipline, which eroded under deadline pressure. Fix: a CI check blocking a PR with new business logic and no new test that fails on main, converting the practice from a request into a policy.

drills.q: Why does contract testing specifically require starting with the highest-incident-cost service boundary rather than rolling out broadly?
drills.a: The provider team has to do the verification work but the consumer team feels most of the pain when it's skipped -- an incentive mismatch. Starting where the provider has recently felt real production pain from a break gives them their own motivation to invest, rather than mandating uncompensated work everywhere at once.

drills.q: A Testcontainers rollout reverts to mocks within a quarter. What's the most likely root cause, and what's the fix?
drills.a: No one owns the shared container-startup infrastructure, so flaky starts (port collisions, image pull timeouts) get blamed on 'the tests' rather than fixed as infrastructure. Fix: assign explicit ownership of the harness with the same seriousness as any shared CI tooling, plus a documented startup-failure runbook.

drills.q: A green, 100%-line-coverage AI-generated test suite let a regression ship anyway. Explain the mechanism and the systematic fix.
drills.a: Tests assert mock-call structure or implementation details rather than observable behavior, so no assertion fails even when the real behavior is wrong -- coverage measures execution, not verification. Systematic fix: run mutation testing (mutmut/Stryker/PIT) periodically against critical modules to measure whether tests actually catch deliberately introduced bugs.

drills.q: An org wants to adopt TDD, contract testing, Testcontainers, and chaos engineering simultaneously as one quality initiative. What's wrong, and how would you sequence it instead?
drills.a: Each practice has a distinct adoption obstacle requiring dedicated organizational attention; doing all four at once dilutes the focus any one needs to stick, producing a 'we tried everything, nothing stuck' outcome. Sequence instead by tracing the org's actual recent incidents to root cause: recurring integration-boundary bugs -> Testcontainers/pyramid work first; cross-service breaking changes -> contract testing first; a fallback path that failed once it mattered -> chaos first; defects in poorly-understood complex logic -> TDD first.

drills.q: Six months after enforcing test-presence gates (new-logic-needs-a-test, contract verification as a deploy gate, Testcontainers as default), a mutation-testing audit shows most tests would still pass against deliberately broken implementations. What does this reveal, and what's the fix?
drills.a: It reveals the expected limit of presence-based gates: they enforce that something got written, not that it's good. This isn't evidence the practices failed -- it's evidence presence and quality need separate enforcement layers. Fix: add a quality-measuring layer on top (mutation-score thresholds in CI, pact matcher-strictness audits, chaos-finding follow-through tracking).

drills.q: Why is chaos engineering's adoption curve steeper than TDD's, contract testing's, or Testcontainers', specifically?
drills.a: The other three can be adopted incrementally with limited downside if done imperfectly. Chaos engineering's prerequisite (observability + fast rollback) must exist BEFORE the practice is safe to run at all -- skipping it and attempting an ambitious first experiment risks turning it into an actual production incident, which reliably kills organizational appetite for the practice afterward.
